issues.detail: The primary booking module promises an action but explicitly downgrades the result to a manual availability enquiry, while no immediate availability state is visible.
issues.evidence: The form CTA reads “CHECK AVAILABILITY,” yet the supporting copy says “Availability enquiry. Dates and final terms are confirmed directly by Mfinity.” The scan reports `bookingSignalCount: 0` and `trustSignalCount: 0`, although the critical journey itself does not technically fail.
issues.expected: A premium rental path makes the commercial model explicit at the point of intent: live availability and a reservable next step, or clearly labelled request-to-book availability with an expected response channel/time and a confident continuation flow.
issues.observed: A user can select dates and a vehicle, but cannot tell whether the result is live inventory, a reservation request, when they will hear back, or what happens next.
issues.recommendation: Rename the action to “Request availability” unless inventory is genuinely live. On submission, provide a vehicle/date-specific next step and response expectation; ideally expose availability status, daily rate/total estimate, deposit and reservation terms before requiring a manual conversation.
issues.title: Booking intent is presented as availability without availability clarity

issues.detail: The opening image is treated so softly that the vehicle is difficult to inspect. Cinematic atmosphere is appropriate, but a luxury rental business is selling the specific car as much as the mood.
issues.evidence: In both supplied hero screenshots, the Ferrari, trees and building are visibly heavily blurred; on mobile the vehicle is largely reduced to a dark/red partial crop. The objective scan confirms vehicle imagery exists (19 images), so this is an art-direction issue rather than missing media.
issues.expected: Reference-quality luxury rental design retains a cinematic hero while keeping a hero vehicle's paint, form, interior or recognizable silhouette crisp enough to communicate real inventory quality.
issues.observed: The visual leads with an indistinct red car and atmospheric blur, reducing product credibility and the premium value carried by the imagery.
issues.recommendation: Use a sharp, professionally art-directed vehicle image as the primary hero layer. Preserve contrast and restrained depth-of-field, but place the focal area around a recognizable vehicle detail and test the mobile crop independently.
issues.title: Hero imagery obscures the product being rented

issues.detail: The page asks for a high-value rental enquiry before establishing the operational proof expected for an unfamiliar premium rental operator.
issues.evidence: The scan records zero trust signals. Visible reassurance is limited to “Nueva Andalucía base · regular inspections & maintenance · direct local contact,” plus a WhatsApp link. No insurance, review/social proof, verified location, delivery coverage, concierge standard, payment/deposit reassurance, or fleet proof is visible in the supplied first viewport.
issues.expected: Reference-quality operators substantiate premium claims with concise, concrete proof close to the enquiry decision: verified local presence, fleet/vehicle condition standards, insured/rental terms, reviews or affiliations, and clear collection/delivery support.
issues.location: Homepage hero, directly below the availability form
issues.observed: The terse operational line feels self-asserted rather than independently credible, particularly for expensive, deposit-led vehicle rental.
issues.recommendation: Add a tightly designed proof strip or nearby reassurance content with factual service credentials, real review evidence, collection/delivery geography, insurance/verification guidance, and a link to complete rental terms. Avoid generic badge clutter.
issues.title: High-consideration enquiry lacks trust proof

issues.detail: Mobile concentrates too much vertical space on hero rhetoric and the enquiry module before allowing meaningful vehicle discovery, despite discovery being a stated secondary goal.
issues.evidence: The supplied mobile screenshot remains within the hero/form treatment at approximately 1,690px tall. The page shows only the beginning of “VEHICLE CARE / FLEET STANDARD” at the bottom; no actual vehicle card is reached. The scan confirms the collection exists but does not indicate a booking or inventory signal.
issues.expected: On mobile, users should be able to start an enquiry quickly while seeing clear fleet discovery within the initial scroll, with compact date controls or a persistent booking action rather than a dominant full-height hero.
issues.observed: The page gives the brand message, form, reassurance copy and two large CTAs priority over seeing cars. The “Explore collection” text is not an obvious compact control in the screenshot.
issues.recommendation: Shorten the mobile hero and move the enquiry form into a compact expandable sheet or follow it immediately with featured vehicle cards. Make “Explore collection” a clearly recognizable action and preserve a sticky availability/enquiry entry point during browsing.
issues.title: Mobile delays access to the actual fleet

issues.detail: The visual language is polished in isolation but internally conflicted: the ornate crest logo signals traditional chauffeur/club luxury while the oversized neo-grotesk type and sharp editorial layout signal contemporary performance luxury.
issues.evidence: The header logo is a detailed crowned “Mfinity” crest, while the hero, labels and CTA system use an austere all-caps/sans-serif editorial treatment. The scan also detects five font families and 66 colors, unusually broad for a minimal luxury system.
issues.expected: A reference-quality luxury identity uses one coherent brand era and tightly governed typography, color and component language across logo, navigation, booking UI and fleet presentation.
issues.observed: The crest appears small and decorative rather than premium and intentional at the scale shown; it competes conceptually with the more modern layout.
issues.recommendation: Choose a deliberate brand direction. Either refine the crest into a confident contemporary mark with a controlled wordmark system, or carry its classic luxury cues consistently through typography and details. Reduce the active font/color vocabulary to a disciplined system.
issues.title: Brand identity and interface styling do not fully agree

issues.detail: The hero presents competing actions without a clear decision hierarchy: explore the collection, check availability, reserve now, WhatsApp, and rent a car all appear within the same initial experience.
issues.evidence: Desktop shows “EXPLORE COLLECTION,” the availability CTA and “RESERVE NOW” in the vehicle panel. Mobile adds two large peer CTAs, “WHATSAPP” and “RENT A CAR,” after the same form. The scan finds four primary CTAs and an inconsistent button ratio of 0.367.
issues.expected: A high-end conversion path gives one unmistakable primary action per context, with a secondary escape route that does not compete visually or semantically.
issues.location: Homepage hero and mobile CTA area
issues.observed: “Reserve now,” “Rent a car,” and “Check availability” imply different stages but do not visibly explain their distinctions. This weakens confidence in the intended path.
issues.recommendation: Define one primary journey, such as “Request availability,” and use a single consistently styled action for it. Keep WhatsApp as a quieter assisted-sales option, and make collection browsing the secondary route. Remove or rename duplicate booking verbs unless each leads to a distinct, explained outcome.
issues.title: Multiple booking labels fragment the primary path

aiReview.summary: Mfinity has a strong editorial starting point and an unusually polished structural baseline, but it is not yet reference-quality for luxury rental conversion. Its major weakness is that the cinematic presentation suppresses the inventory, and the central form behaves like a request flow without sufficiently clear availability, commercial next steps or trust proof. Tightening the brand system, elevating sharp real vehicle photography, and designing a more explicit request-to-book journey would materially improve perceived value and enquiry confidence.
strengths: The hero establishes Marbella, premium mobility and a featured supercar immediately; it has a deliberate cinematic ambition rather than a generic rental-directory presentation.
The desktop availability form is prominent, structured around the essential initial fields, and visually integrated into the hero rather than buried below marketing content.
Mobile has no visible horizontal overflow, tap targets appear comfortably sized, and the header is pared down appropriately for the narrow viewport.
Typography has strong scale and contrast in the hero, making the brand proposition immediately legible despite the image treatment.
The scan supports solid baseline execution: no broken internal links or console errors, complete image alt coverage, coherent heading structure, legal/privacy links, and a fast loading experience.

issues.detail: The main above-the-fold visit path asks users to “Visítanos hoy” but does not make the decision easy at the moment of intent. For a destination café in Puerto Banús, hours, precise address/map context, and a one-tap contact route are core visit information, not secondary details.
issues.evidence: The desktop and mobile hero show “Visítanos hoy” and “Marbella · Spain,” but neither screenshot shows opening hours, a street/location reference, phone/WhatsApp, or map cue. The scan records only one contact signal and zero booking signals.
issues.expected: A reference-quality hospitality homepage makes immediate visit viability visible: exact Puerto Banús location, today’s opening status/hours, and a clear map, call, or WhatsApp action near the visit CTA.
issues.observed: The location is reduced to a broad city-and-country label, while the most useful visit details are absent from the primary decision area.
issues.recommendation: Turn the secondary visit CTA into a direct visit module or destination page that surfaces address, opening hours, directions, and a mobile-native contact action. Use “Puerto Banús” consistently as the geographic anchor rather than relying on “Marbella · Spain.”
issues.title: The primary visit journey lacks operational certainty

issues.detail: The hero is venue-led rather than product-led. It communicates a polished interior, but the pastries that establish premium pâtisserie craft are small, behind reflective glass, or peripheral. This weakens appetite appeal and makes the brand feel closer to a well-designed café template than a distinctive food destination.
issues.evidence: In the desktop screenshot, the display case is visually busy and partially obscured by reflection, while the plated products occupy a small area at lower right. In the mobile crop, the most prominent visual elements are shelving, counter equipment, a juice glass, and a cropped table; the pastry selection is not clearly inspectable.
issues.expected: Premium pâtisserie execution should lead with controlled, appetising close-up product imagery alongside enough venue context to establish the place. Products should remain legible and desirable at every responsive crop.
issues.observed: The strongest visual asset is a broad interior shot; the food is not given sufficient scale, clarity, or visual priority.
issues.recommendation: Use an art-directed mobile hero image or crop that gives one or two finished signature products clear prominence. Reserve the wider interior image for a later venue/story section, and use product-focused photography to support the menu CTA.
issues.title: Hero imagery underplays the actual premium product

issues.detail: The headline has a clean, memorable rhythm, but “No sugar. Same taste.” is a broad category claim without enough immediate proof of why Zùsto is credible, distinctive, or worth visiting over other premium cafés. The supporting paragraph stays similarly general.
issues.evidence: Visible hero copy is limited to the claim and “Pastelería artesanal, café y una forma más consciente de disfrutar lo dulce…”. The scan finds zero trust signals despite a premium food-and-wellness positioning.
issues.expected: Reference-quality positioning pairs an emotional brand line with concise substantiation: the pâtissier or method, ingredient philosophy, signature offering, or an independently meaningful quality cue.
issues.observed: The copy establishes the no-sugar proposition but does not demonstrate craft, provenance, specialty, or social proof at the point it needs to justify a premium choice.
issues.recommendation: Add a short proof layer near the opening proposition, such as the chef-led craft, signature sugar-free process, ingredient standards, or a credible endorsement/review signal. Keep the editorial tone, but make the promise concrete.
issues.title: Premium claim is stronger than its proof

issues.detail: The mobile header gives too much space to the language toggle and outlined Contacto button while leaving the navigation dependent on an unlabeled hamburger. The brand descriptor “café by Eric” also disappears at the smaller breakpoint, reducing authorship and differentiation.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows ZÙSTO, “ES / EN,” a large outlined “CONTACTO” control, and a hamburger. The scan identifies the “ERIC” navigation link as the only undersized interactive target at 32.5px wide, below conventional touch comfort.
issues.expected: A reference-quality mobile header preserves essential brand cues while prioritising the key local action and providing comfortably sized, clearly discoverable navigation controls.
issues.observed: Contact has visual priority, but navigation hierarchy and the Eric attribution are weakened; the standalone ERIC link is also unusually narrow for a touch target.
issues.recommendation: Make the menu control explicitly accessible and comfortably sized, increase the ERIC link’s hit area or incorporate it into the concept/brand story, and reassess whether the language switcher merits equal header prominence to the primary visit action.
issues.title: Mobile navigation hierarchy is not fully resolved

issues.detail: The interaction styling lacks a fully unified system. The scan reports an inconsistent-button ratio of 30.8%, and the hero demonstrates several competing CTA treatments: a filled rectangular menu button, a text link with underline, and an outlined pill-shaped Contacto button.
issues.evidence: Desktop and mobile screenshots visibly use three distinct CTA treatments in the same first viewport. The DOM scan reports inconsistentButtonRatio: 0.3077.
issues.expected: A premium editorial site can use hierarchy, but each action type should have a deliberate, repeatable visual role: one primary treatment, one secondary treatment, and restrained utility/navigation styling.
issues.observed: The hierarchy is understandable, but the mix of filled, underlined, and pill-outline treatments reads more assembled than art-directed.
issues.recommendation: Define a clear CTA taxonomy and apply it consistently. For example, reserve the filled treatment for primary conversion, use a single text-arrow treatment for secondary exploration, and keep header contact aligned with that system rather than introducing an unrelated pill form.
issues.title: CTA language is visually inconsistent

issues.detail: The site has no visible trust layer despite asking visitors to choose a premium, health-adjacent food proposition. This leaves the brand story carrying all persuasion without third-party or operational reassurance.
issues.evidence: The scan records trustSignalCount: 0. No ratings, press mentions, customer testimonials, chef credentials, recognisable partners, or review-platform signals are present in the supplied page evidence.
issues.expected: High-performing premium hospitality sites use a restrained proof layer that validates the proposition without compromising editorial restraint.
issues.observed: There is no visible corroboration of quality, popularity, or specialist credibility.
issues.recommendation: Introduce one carefully designed trust section after the concept or menu preview: selected review quotation/rating, press recognition, chef expertise, or evidence of ingredients and process. Avoid generic logo walls or excessive testimonials.
issues.title: No trust signals support the premium positioning

aiReview.summary: Zùsto Café has a strong technical foundation and a polished first impression, but the current homepage falls short of reference-quality premium pâtisserie work because it sells atmosphere more effectively than food, proof, and visit certainty. The immediate opportunity is to make signature products visually irresistible on mobile, substantiate the no-sugar promise, and bring practical visit information into the primary journey. Those changes would improve both the perceived value of the brand and the likelihood that an interested visitor converts into an in-person visit.
strengths: The first viewport is visually polished and immediately conveys a real, upscale café environment rather than a generic stock-led hospitality site.
The brand, no-sugar proposition, location cue, menu path, and visit path are all discoverable above the fold.
Typography creates a credible editorial contrast between the display headline and restrained navigational copy.
The Spanish-language presentation is coherent for the local market, while the visible ES / EN control acknowledges an international Puerto Banús audience.

The measured foundation is exceptionally strong: fast load and LCP, negligible layout shift, no horizontal overflow, complete image alt coverage, valid page structure, no detected errors, and strong geo/SEO essentials.
The mobile layout preserves the core message and primary menu action without visible clipping or structural breakage.

issues.expected: Professional buyers should be able to assess fit without hunting through several pages: vehicle capacity, use cases, geography, accessibility, staffing or operation model, timing, and what information is needed for a quote.

issues.observed: The writing communicates atmosphere and experience better than scope, constraints, and deliverables. “Conocer los vehículos” is useful but does not replace a concise comparison of available options.

issues.detail: The mobile hero is visually dramatic but consumes almost the entire first viewport before the user reaches any service or proof content.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows the header, eyebrow, four-line headline, three-line description, and two full-width CTA buttons before the yellow section boundary at the bottom. The primary content below the fold is not previewed.
issues.expected: Mobile should preserve the emotional impact while giving users an early indication of services, proof, or a second actionable route. Lead-oriented pages need fast orientation and progression.
issues.observed: The page is readable and there is no horizontal overflow, but the amount of vertical space devoted to the hero delays the information a buyer needs to qualify the offer.
issues.recommendation: Shorten the mobile hero copy, reduce vertical spacing, and let the next section or a compact proof strip enter the viewport. Keep one dominant CTA and make the secondary vehicle-discovery action visually subordinate.

issues.detail: The mobile navigation exposes only a hamburger icon, so important destinations and the contact route are hidden at the moment when the page most needs to reduce friction.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows no visible navigation labels and no contact or quote destination besides the hero buttons. The scan reports 14 navigation links but zero contact signals.
issues.expected: The menu should make the lead route prominent and provide a clear information architecture for services, vehicles, company proof, and contact, with the primary action easy to reach after opening it.
issues.observed: The hamburger is recognizable, but the screenshot offers no persistent contact affordance and gives no indication of what is inside the menu.
issues.recommendation: Keep a compact quote/contact action in the mobile header or immediately below it. In the opened menu, group links by buyer intent and surface “Solicitar presupuesto” first, followed by services, vehicles, projects, and company information.
issues.title: Contact path is hidden on mobile

issues.detail: The visual direction is coherent and distinctive, but the homepage leans heavily on a dark hero treatment and a single yellow accent, reducing depth and making the overall system feel closer to a polished template than an established specialist brand.
issues.evidence: The supplied desktop and mobile screenshots are dominated by one red vehicle image, a black overlay, white typography, and yellow accents. The visible header, CTA, and diagonal yellow hero boundary are all highly stylized, while no broader brand or portfolio system is visible in the first viewport.
issues.expected: Reference quality should retain the strong transport identity while demonstrating a richer, more ownable visual language across proof, services, fleet, and enquiry sections.
issues.observed: The hero looks intentional, but the first impression is primarily a campaign statement. It does not yet communicate the breadth, maturity, or operational credibility expected from a specialist supplier.
issues.recommendation: Use the hero as the entry point to a more evidence-led system: real project photography, annotated vehicle details, route or deployment imagery, restrained graphic motifs, and consistent section layouts that make the portfolio feel proprietary rather than merely styled.

issues.expected: Reference-quality typography should establish a controlled type scale with comfortable reading sizes, clear hierarchy, and consistent button treatment across navigation, labels, cards, and calls to action.

issues.observed: The oversized headline is legible, but the supporting system becomes visually compressed and overly art-directed. Small all-caps labels add style without enough practical scanning value.

aiReview.summary: Trenes y Tranvías has a strong first impression: the real vehicle imagery, black-white-yellow palette, and editorial headline create a distinctive transport brand rather than a generic services page. The visual polish is ahead of the commercial communication. The critical weakness is conversion readiness: there is no visible form, direct contact signal, trust proof, or substantive qualification information, despite the business targeting high-consideration municipal, event, and venue enquiries. The next version should preserve the confident hero while bringing the actual offer, evidence, local credibility, and enquiry mechanism into the first scroll, especially on mobile.
strengths: The hero immediately communicates the product category through a real red tourist train, rather than relying on abstract illustration or generic stock imagery.
The headline has a distinctive voice and a memorable promise: “La ciudad se disfruta a bordo.” It creates emotional differentiation for a transport-experience business.
The primary and secondary actions are visually clear, with strong contrast and a sensible split between project enquiry and vehicle discovery.
The desktop composition has a confident editorial hierarchy, and the mobile layout avoids horizontal overflow while keeping the headline and CTAs readable.
The navigation structure and page headings are reasonably organized, with a single H1 and clear service, vehicle, company, and management destinations.
The site is fast and technically stable according to the scan, so the main opportunity is commercial clarity and trust rather than page performance.

issues.title: The primary charter configurator does not communicate enough interaction or booking value on mobile
issues.detail: On mobile, the main conversion surface resembles a five-cell itinerary summary. Only the date has a calendar icon; "2 guests," "Half day · 4h," "Puerto Banus," and "Private yacht day" appear as static text without chevrons, buttons, selected-state cues, or explanatory microcopy. issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows a large two-column grid with only a date icon as an explicit affordance. The scan confirms the site has one form and six booking signals, but does not provide evidence that these individual choices are visibly actionable.
issues.observed: A buyer can see default selections but has weak visual evidence about what can be changed, what happens next, or whether the result is an availability request versus an immediate booking.
issues.expected: Reference-quality charter UX makes every configurable selection visibly interactive, presents a short, unmistakable next-step path, and uses the enquiry surface to reduce uncertainty before contact.
issues.location: Homepage hero charter panel, especially mobile.
issues.recommendation: Use consistently interactive field treatments for party size, date, duration, departure, and occasion, with clear disclosure indicators and active/focus states. Change the submission label to a precise commercial outcome such as "Check availability" or "Request a tailored charter," then state the response expectation adjacent to it.

issues.title: The premium claim lacks independent trust proof
issues.detail: The visible reassurance layer consists of self-authored claims: "15+ years local experience," "Real availability," and "Qualified skipper." These are useful operational statements but are not evidence of reputation, licensing, safety standards, service quality, or local standing. For a high-consideration charter purchase, this creates a gap between the luxury positioning and the proof presented.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports trustSignalCount: 0. The screenshots show only internal assertions in the black reassurance band and no reviews, ratings, partner/operator credentials, press, awards, client proof, or safety/insurance markers.
issues.observed: The site asks visitors to trust the operator without showing a third-party or verifiable reason to do so.
issues.expected: A reference luxury charter proposition pairs elegant restraint with a small number of specific, credible proof points that reduce perceived booking risk.
issues.location: Homepage, directly below the enquiry module and in the path into fleet/detail pages.
issues.recommendation: Add a restrained trust module using genuine assets only: review source and rating, verified operating history, skipper/operating credentials, safety or insurance standards, and a concise statement on who handles the booking. Place the most consequential proof near the enquiry CTA and repeat relevant proof on yacht pages.

issues.title: Pricing context is too faint and incomplete at the moment of intent
issues.detail: Desktop shows "Sunseeker 68 · from €4,375 / 4h" only in the low-contrast lower reassurance strip, followed by "low season · 21% VAT excluded." Mobile does not show this price in the captured hero. The lone figure is not tied to the user's chosen party, date, duration, or inclusions, and the tax exclusion introduces ambiguity rather than confidence.
issues.evidence: The desktop screenshot places the price in the smallest text area of the darkest band. The scan identifies pricing only incidentally through visible content and reports no trust signals; the mobile first viewport ends before equivalent pricing is visible.
issues.observed: A user is invited to find a charter before receiving usable budget framing, while the one available price has qualifying information that can make the final cost feel uncertain.
issues.expected: Reference-quality luxury charter sites provide an elegant but concrete "from" price, duration, tax treatment, and key inclusion/exclusion context before an enquiry, while preserving a tailored-service model.
issues.location: Homepage hero enquiry and immediate follow-up content; mobile first viewport.
issues.recommendation: Show a clear, legible indicative range or starting price linked to the selected duration, with "VAT included/excluded" handled plainly and key inclusions summarized. Make it clear where final availability and bespoke pricing may vary.

issues.title: Mobile hero crop and hierarchy obscure the aspirational product
issues.detail: The mobile composition gives the location line, very large four-line headline, and long supporting paragraph most of the first 865 pixels. The yacht is largely reduced to a partial, low-contrast background fragment at the left and bottom. The page therefore reads more like a text-led editorial masthead than a vivid yacht-charter invitation.
issues.evidence: In the mobile screenshot, the yacht is only partially discernible behind the copy and configurator, while the headline occupies four large lines. The desktop screenshot demonstrates that the same source image can present the yacht much more clearly.
issues.observed: The actual high-value product is not easily inspectable in the primary mobile decision moment.
issues.expected: A reference luxury mobile hero retains a clear, desirable view of the vessel or experience while preserving concise positioning and an immediate enquiry route.
issues.recommendation: Create a mobile-specific hero crop or image treatment that holds a recognizable yacht silhouette and more open water. Tighten the location line and supporting copy, reduce the display headline footprint modestly, and position the enquiry entry point so the image still has visual authority.

issues.title: The homepage tells an attractive story but does not yet answer enough purchase-critical questions
issues.detail: The visible proposition mentions private charter, sailing, fishing, group experiences, local experience, availability, skipper, and one starting price. It does not visibly establish practical buyer considerations such as guest capacity, sample itinerary, what is included, weather/cancellation handling, departure logistics, or why this operator's fleet is distinctive.
issues.evidence: The scan records 678 words, three featured yachts, destination pages, and a single form. The screenshot's visible content is primarily brand statement, form defaults, and short operational claims.
issues.observed: Visitors receive mood and broad category coverage, but limited evidence to compare options or feel ready to enquire for an expensive day charter.
issues.expected: A reference charter homepage uses concise editorial copy plus scannable decision support, then directs visitors naturally to individual vessels and experiences.
issues.location: Homepage content immediately following the hero and fleet discovery entries.
issues.recommendation: Add concise, high-value decision content around the fleet and experience links: capacity and ideal use case, price/duration starting points, included crew/fuel/catering notes where applicable, departure ports, and clear weather/cancellation expectations. Preserve the editorial tone; this does not require turning the page into a dense FAQ.

issues.title: CTA language fragments the single charter journey
issues.detail: The page exposes "Plan a charter" in the header and sticky mobile bar, "Find my charter" on the main configurator, and "WhatsApp" as an equally prominent mobile action. These are all defensible routes, but their distinct wording implies different outcomes without explaining the distinction.
issues.evidence: Both screenshots show "Plan a charter" and "Find my charter" for the core path; the mobile screenshot additionally presents a large WhatsApp button. The scan counts four primary CTAs and six booking signals.
issues.observed: Visitors must infer whether they are planning, searching, requesting availability, or starting a chat, which weakens the otherwise controlled experience.
issues.expected: Reference-quality conversion design gives one primary action a stable name and deliberately positions alternate contact methods as secondary channels with a clear purpose.
issues.location: Desktop header and hero; mobile sticky action bar.
issues.recommendation: Standardize the central CTA around the actual workflow, for example "Check availability" or "Plan your charter." Keep WhatsApp as a secondary assisted-contact route and label its expected use clearly through its surrounding context or destination.

aiReview.summary: The first viewport is polished and clearly above commodity charter-site execution: restrained editorial typography, a real yacht image, coherent dark-and-ivory palette, and strong desktop composition establish an aspirational tone. However, it stops short of reference-quality luxury charter conversion. The mobile hero prioritizes atmosphere and oversized copy over usable fleet proof, pricing clarity, and confidence-building detail; the enquiry configurator reads more like a styled summary than a clearly interactive booking tool. The scan confirms excellent technical and accessibility foundations, but the commercial trust and decision support required for an expensive, location-sensitive charter remain underdeveloped.
strengths: The hero uses actual yacht photography rather than a generic abstract luxury treatment, and the desktop image, muted overlay, serif display type, and compact navigation create a credible premium editorial direction.
The business and location are immediately legible. The desktop eyebrow names Marbella, Puerto Banus, and Costa del Sol, while the headline is concise and memorable.
The desktop charter path is prominent: a substantial, above-the-fold enquiry module and a clear "Find my charter" action support the primary goal without forcing a long scroll.
Mobile navigation is appropriately simplified to a phone number and menu trigger, while the sticky "Plan a charter" and "WhatsApp" actions preserve contact routes.

The page has unusually strong underlying hygiene for a marketing site: no broken links, no console or network failures, no horizontal overflow, labeled controls, a valid heading structure, and fast desktop/mobile loading metrics.

There is meaningful fleet and destination architecture behind the homepage, including individual yacht, destination, experiences, owner, contact, booking, and guide URLs rather than a single thin landing page.

aiReview.summary: Marbella For Sale has a credible luxury aesthetic and a technically clean foundation, but the first-viewport experience currently behaves more like a brand film than a premium property platform. The largest commercial gap is the weak visibility of the enquiry path; the largest design gap is the amount of dark overlay and mobile hero space used before visitors reach practical property information. The automated scores are strong, but qualitative execution is not reference quality because the site has not yet converted its visual polish into clear trust, discovery, and enquiry momentum.

The visual direction has a restrained editorial intent with strong use of whitespace, uppercase micro-labels, and a controlled premium palette.
The site has a coherent information architecture spanning properties, developments, areas, selling, guides, about, and contact.
The objective scan confirms a stable baseline: no horizontal overflow, no broken internal links, one clear H1, complete image alt coverage, no console errors, and strong measured loading performance.

aiReview.summary: La Bocana has a polished, credible editorial foundation and strong technical delivery, but it is not yet reference-quality for a premium destination restaurant. The initial consent takeover materially harms the most important mobile moment, practical booking information is too deferred, and the trust and culinary proof are thinner than the luxury positioning warrants. Resolving those points while tightening reservation nomenclature would turn a visually attractive experience into a more decisive booking tool.
strengths: The core visual direction is appropriate for Puerto Banús: understated editorial serif display type, waterfront dining photography, a restrained palette, and generous composition avoid an overtly generic restaurant template.
The desktop hero has a clear premium atmosphere and makes the location immediately legible with “Puerto Banús · Marbella.”
The primary reservation action is visible in both desktop and mobile headers, and the mobile header reserves substantial space for it.
Navigation has clear routes to the menu, house story, gallery, contact, reservations, and language selection.
Objective quality is strong: fast load metrics, no layout shift, no horizontal overflow, accessible interactive targets, complete image alt coverage, and no detected broken links or console errors.

aiReview.summary: The supplied site is not reviewable as a premium real-estate experience because the homepage never visibly progresses beyond a loader on either desktop or mobile. The business-critical surfaces are absent: brand positioning, property inventory, imagery, navigation, filters, trust proof and enquiry capture. The strong automated performance and viewport measurements describe an efficient empty shell, not a successful customer experience. The first priority is to make the real homepage render reliably, then establish a property-led discovery and enquiry journey.
strengths: The automated scan reports strong delivery fundamentals: HTTP 200, fast measured loading, minimal layout shift, no horizontal overflow, no console or network failures, and valid viewport metadata.

The scan also reports complete image alt coverage for the currently rendered DOM and no tiny tap targets, although the lack of rendered imagery and controls limits the practical significance of those checks.
The restrained burgundy and copper combination could become a distinctive premium palette if it is applied to a complete, property-led interface rather than a persistent loading screen.
